guide.summary: The most persuasive arguments take opposing views seriously. This final unit covers how writers introduce, concede, refute, and qualify in response to alternative perspectives, and how doing so builds credibility and complexity. It is also the unit most tied to the sophistication point in all three essays.

sections.heading: Why address counterarguments
Ways to respond
sections.body:
- **Refutation:** show the counterargument is wrong (bad evidence, faulty logic).
- **Concession:** grant part of it is true.
- **Concession + rebuttal:** grant it, then show it doesn't defeat the thesis ("Yes, the program is costly; but the cost of inaction is higher").
- **Qualification:** adjust your claim to account for it ("in most cases," "for schools with...").
- **Reframing:** show the opposing view answers a different question than the one that matters.

Writers signal these moves with phrases like *admittedly, granted, critics argue, it is true that, yet, nevertheless, this objection overlooks*.

sections.heading: Placement
sections.body: Counterarguments can appear early (to clear the ground), in the middle (as one step in a line of reasoning), or near the end (to show the thesis survives scrutiny). Ending on the counterargument without a response is a common error: the audience's last impression is the opposing view.

sections.heading: Counterarguments and Row C
sections.body: The sophistication point often goes to essays that explore complexity: acknowledging tensions, limits, and competing values. A thoughtful concession that sharpens rather than weakens your thesis is one of the most reliable ways to earn it. In rhetorical analysis, explaining how a writer handles opposition and why that handling suits the audience can also show complex understanding of the rhetorical situation.

keyTakeaways: Address the strongest opposing view, not a straw man.
Responses include refutation, concession, rebuttal, qualification, and reframing.
Concessions build credibility if followed by a response.
Don't end on an unanswered counterargument.
Handling opposition well is a key path to the sophistication point.
Signal phrases help readers follow the move.
commonMistakes: Attacking a weak version of the opposing argument.
Conceding so much that the thesis collapses.
Mentioning a counterargument with no response.
Treating every counterargument as completely wrong.
Confusing a concession with changing your position.
In rhetorical analysis, naming "counterargument" without explaining its effect on the audience.
examTips: Plan one serious counterargument for each argument and synthesis essay.
Use a source that disagrees with you in synthesis, then answer it.
MCQs often ask about the function of a concession; it usually prepares a rebuttal.
Watch for distractors claiming the writer "agrees with" an opponent when the writer only concedes part.
Qualification counts as complexity only if it's sustained, not tacked on.
guide.cramSheet:
**Why:** ethos · preempt · reframe

**Moves:** refute · concede · concede + rebut · qualify · reframe

**Signals:** admittedly · granted · critics argue · yet · nevertheless · this overlooks

**Avoid:** straw man · unanswered ending · over-concession

**Row C:** complexity through tensions and limits

vocab.definition: An argument opposing the writer's claim.
Acknowledging that part of an opposing argument is valid.
A response showing why a counterargument doesn't defeat the writer's claim.
Demonstrating that a counterargument is incorrect.
A weak or distorted version of an opponent's argument, set up to be easily defeated.
Presenting the strongest version of an opposing argument before responding.
Shifting the terms of a debate to show the opposing view addresses the wrong question.
Limiting a claim's scope to account for exceptions or opposing evidence.
Addressing an objection before the audience raises it.
A different viewpoint on an issue, not necessarily directly opposed.
Recognition of tensions, limits, and competing values in an issue.
Credibility, strengthened by fair treatment of opposing views.

practice.stimulus: Admittedly, banning gas-powered leaf blowers will make yard work slower for landscaping crews. But the noise and exhaust fall on every household on the block, while the extra time falls on businesses that can adjust their prices.
practice.stem: The word "Admittedly" signals that the writer is

choices.text: conceding a point before rebutting it
changing positions
introducing a statistic
summarizing the conclusion

practice.explanation: "Admittedly" grants a cost; "But" introduces the rebuttal.

distractors.B: The writer keeps supporting the ban.

practice.stimulus: Opponents of the bike lane apparently believe that cars should rule every inch of the city and that anyone on two wheels deserves to be run over.
practice.stem: The writer's characterization of the opponents is best described as

choices.text: a straw man that distorts the opposing view
a fair concession
a qualified claim
steelmanning

practice.explanation: Few opponents hold this extreme view; distorting it makes it easy to dismiss but persuades no actual opponent.

practice.stimulus: Original claim: "Online classes are worse than in-person classes." After reading research showing that online classes work well for self-motivated adult learners, the writer revises the claim.
practice.stem: Which revision best qualifies the claim in response to the research?

choices.text: For most high school students, in-person classes produce better outcomes than online ones, though online learning can work well for self-motivated adults.
Online classes are always worse.
Online classes are better than in-person classes for everyone.
Classes exist in different formats.

practice.explanation: It limits the claim's scope and acknowledges where the opposing evidence applies.

distractors.C: Abandons the position rather than qualifying it.

practice.stimulus: An essay arguing for a four-day school week ends: "Of course, critics point out that working parents will struggle to find childcare on the fifth day."
practice.stem: What is the main problem with this ending?

choices.text: It ends on an unanswered counterargument, leaving the audience with the opposing view.
It concedes too little.
It uses too many statistics.
It refutes a straw man.

practice.explanation: Without a response, the final impression undermines the writer's thesis.

distractors.D: The concern is real and fairly stated.

practice.stimulus: Critics of free school meals for all students ask why wealthy families should get a free lunch. It is a fair question, but it misses what universal meals are for. When every student eats free, no child stands in a separate line, no form goes unreturned, and the cafeteria stops sorting children by their parents' income.
practice.stem: The writer's response to the critics is best described as

choices.text: reframing, arguing that the program's purpose is to remove stigma and barriers rather than to target only the needy
a complete concession to the critics
a statistical refutation
a straw man

practice.explanation: The writer grants the question is "fair" but argues it addresses the wrong goal.

practice.stimulus: It is true that rent control can discourage new construction when it applies to all buildings. That is why the proposal before the council exempts any building completed in the last fifteen years.
practice.stem: The writer's concession primarily serves to

choices.text: acknowledge a well-known criticism and show the proposal was designed to avoid it
argue against rent control
change the subject to construction
introduce a personal anecdote

practice.explanation: The concession sets up the exemption as an answer, building credibility.

practice.stimulus: A writer arguing for a downtown homeless shelter wants to address opponents fairly before responding.
practice.stem: Which sentence best presents the strongest version of the opposing view?

choices.text: Opponents worry, reasonably, that a shelter without enough staff or services could concentrate problems in one neighborhood rather than solve them.
Opponents simply don't care about homeless people.
Opponents are worried about nothing.
Some people have opinions.

practice.explanation: It states a serious, specific concern that real opponents hold.

practice.stimulus: Opponents claim that wind turbines kill so many birds that they are worse for wildlife than fossil fuels. But estimates from wildlife agencies suggest that turbines kill far fewer birds each year than collisions with buildings or attacks by domestic cats, and climate change threatens far more species.
practice.stem: The writer's response is primarily a

choices.text: refutation that puts the opponents' concern in comparative context
concession that turbines are worse for birds
personal anecdote
qualification of the writer's own thesis

practice.explanation: Comparing turbine deaths with larger causes and with climate risk challenges the claim that turbines are worse overall.

practice.stimulus:
Draft paragraph arguing that schools should eliminate class rank: "Class rank creates unhealthy competition. Students avoid challenging electives to protect their GPAs. Schools should eliminate it."

The writer wants to add a sentence acknowledging an alternative perspective that colleges value.
practice.stem: Which sentence would best do this before the final recommendation?

choices.text: Some admissions officers say rank helps them compare applicants from unfamiliar schools, but most colleges now rely on school profiles that provide that context without ranking students.
Class rank is mathematically simple to calculate.
Everyone hates class rank.
Many students take electives.

practice.explanation: It presents a real reason for rank and answers it, supporting the recommendation.

distractors.C: Overgeneralizes and offers no alternative perspective.

practice.stimulus:
Thesis: Cities should build more public housing.
Draft concession: "Critics are right that public housing has failed everywhere it has been tried and always becomes a center of crime."
practice.stem: What is the main problem with this concession?

choices.text: It concedes an absolute claim that, if true, would defeat the writer's thesis.
It is too brief.
It uses a statistic.
It refutes the critics too strongly.

practice.explanation: Granting that public housing "always" fails leaves no room for the argument; a better concession would acknowledge specific past failures and their causes.

practice.stimulus: Those who oppose the new trail are not wrong that it will bring more people into the woods behind their homes. They are wrong to assume that people who come to see a forest will want to harm it. The best protection a forest has is a public that has walked in it.
practice.stem: The passage's handling of the opposition is most effective because it

choices.text: grants the opponents' factual claim while challenging the assumption behind their conclusion, then turns their concern into an argument for the trail
dismisses the opponents as selfish
provides statistics on forest damage
concedes that the trail should not be built

practice.explanation: The writer separates the true premise (more visitors) from the faulty inference (harm) and reframes visitors as protectors.

practice.stimulus: Skeptics ask whether the city can afford to plant ten thousand trees. The better question is whether it can afford another summer like the last one, when heat sent four hundred residents to the emergency room and air conditioning bills drove families into debt.
practice.stem: The writer's strategy is best described as

choices.text: reframing the cost question by comparing the expense of planting with the costs of not planting
conceding that the trees are unaffordable
refuting the skeptics with a personal anecdote
attacking the skeptics' character

practice.explanation: "The better question" shifts the frame from affordability of action to the costs of inaction.

practice.stimulus: A student writing to classmates argues that the school should replace letter grades with written feedback. She expects her audience, who worry about college admissions, to resist.
practice.stem: Which counterargument strategy would most likely persuade this audience?

choices.text: Acknowledge the admissions worry directly and explain how colleges evaluate students from schools that already use narrative evaluations.
Ignore admissions entirely and focus on philosophy.
Tell classmates that worrying about college is shallow.
Argue that colleges don't matter.

practice.explanation: Addressing the audience's main concern with specific reassurance answers the objection they're already raising.

practice.stimulus:
Thesis A: "Standardized testing should be abolished."
Thesis B: "Standardized tests measure some skills reliably, but because scores track family income closely, colleges should weigh them alongside context rather than treat them as decisive."
practice.stem: Which statement best explains why Thesis B shows more complexity?

choices.text: It acknowledges the tests' strengths and limits and proposes a position that accounts for both.
It is longer than Thesis A.
It avoids taking any position.
It agrees completely with supporters of testing.

practice.explanation: Complexity comes from weighing competing considerations while still taking a clear position.

distractors.C: Thesis B takes a clear position on how colleges should use scores.

practice.stimulus:
The following passage is from a letter, written for this practice set, by a high school principal to parents who opposed the school's decision to require all ninth graders to take a semester-long financial literacy course.

I have read every one of your emails, and I want to begin with what many of you got right. You worry that another required course will crowd out electives your children love. You are correct that it will, for one semester. You worry that this is the kind of thing families should teach at home. In many of your homes, I have no doubt it is.

But I have also read a different set of letters. They come from former students, some of them five or six years out of this building. One writes that she signed a car loan at nineteen without understanding what an interest rate was. Another, a young man who was valedictorian, writes that he learned what a credit score was when his first apartment application was rejected. Neither came from a careless family. Both came from families that assumed someone else had covered it.

That is the problem with leaving this to chance: the families most confident it is being handled are not always right, and the students who most need it are the least likely to choose it. A requirement is the only way to make sure it reaches all of them.

We will not take away the arts. We have moved the course into a semester that already held a study hall for most ninth graders. And I promise you this: if, after two years, the course is not doing what I have described, I will come back to you and say so.
practice.prompt:
Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices the principal makes to persuade parents to accept the new requirement.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that analyzes the writer's rhetorical choices.
- Select and use evidence to support your line of reasoning.
- Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Demonstrate an understanding of the rhetorical situation.
- Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

rubric.description: Defensible thesis analyzing the principal's rhetorical choices.
4: specific evidence for all claims with commentary consistently explaining how choices persuade skeptical parents. 3: most claims. 2: mostly summary. 1: little analysis.
E.g., explains how the principal's concessions and promise respond to the parents' distrust; vivid analysis of the rhetorical situation.

practice.sampleResponse:
Writing to parents who have flooded her inbox with objections, the principal disarms resistance by conceding their strongest points, answers them with testimony from former students whose families resembled theirs, and closes with practical reassurances and a promise that make the requirement feel accountable rather than imposed.

The letter opens not with defense but with agreement. "I want to begin with what many of you got right," the principal writes, and she grants that the course "will" crowd out electives and that many families do teach finance at home. For an angry audience, this concession is strategic: parents who expected to be dismissed find themselves validated, and their guard lowers. The phrase "I have read every one of your emails" adds to her ethos as a listener rather than an administrator issuing orders.

The pivot, "But I have also read a different set of letters," mirrors the opening sentence, placing former students' voices beside the parents' own. The examples are chosen with care. A valedictorian whose apartment application was rejected undercuts the assumption that smart, successful students will figure it out. The principal's sentence "Neither came from a careless family" anticipates the parents' instinct to think the problem belongs to other households, and "Both came from families that assumed someone else had covered it" turns that very confidence into the risk.

She then states her reasoning plainly: the families "most confident" are "not always right," and the students who need the course most are "least likely to choose it." This explains why a requirement, rather than an elective, is necessary, answering the parents' implicit question about why the school can't simply offer it.

Finally, the principal addresses the practical fear with specifics: the course replaces a study hall, and "We will not take away the arts." Her closing promise to return and admit failure if the course doesn't work offers parents something rare in a policy letter: accountability. By ending on a commitment rather than a demand, she makes acceptance feel like a trial in which parents remain judges.
